JAPANESE MILL STRIKE AND BOLSHEVISM.

Police investigation failed to disclose any proof
that the strike in question in its primary stage was
anything but the result of a real or imaginary grievance.
It was only after the trouble started that the interest
of the Communists and professional agitators was aroused
sufficiently to cause them to rush in, to assume direction
and control and to constitute themselves representatives
of the workmen and appoint themselves mediators. The
recognition of these persons at a time when the strike
was virtually broken, was rather unfortunate because it
enabled them to escape the discredit which they saw the
failure of the strike was likely to bring upon them, and
it has undoubtedly strengthened their position in the
work which they are now doing of making preparation for
future trouble.
So far from the recent strikes in Japanese
Cotton Mills here being the beginning of an extension
of the Bolshevik campaign in China, Police records show
that movements of this description, with which Bolshevik
activities have been strongly intermingled, started in
this country as far back as 1916, and that at least, as far
as the Settlement is concerned, far from permitting a
campaign of this description to proceed uninterfered with,
the Police, under great difficulties, have done and are
still doing everything in their power to control the
movement which obviously cannot be suppressed if, as is the
case now, it goes on unchecked in those parts of China
with which Shanghai is in constant and direct communication.
Any constructive policy which would help the Police
in their work of suppression to be of any value at all
should take the shape of a legislative enactment such as

2
the following telegram indicates the Peking Government is alleged
has been considering, but has not yet promulgated.
"Peking, Feb. 24, 1925.
"The Ministry of Justice has enacted a law
for the control of Chinese Communists, the gist of
which is as follows :
(1) Anyone who advocates Communism shall be
sentenced to penal servitude ranging from five to
10 years.
(2) Anyone who disturbs public peace or infuses
radical thoughts into or instigates the people shall
be sentenced to penal servitude for the same period
as provided above.
(3) Anyone who is engaged in the propaganda of
Communism or is guilty of any outrageous conduct shall
be sentenced to penal servitude ranging from 10 to 15
years.
(4) Anyone who utilizes the Communism shall be
sentenced to penal servitude ranging from three to five
years.
(5) Anyone, who, guilty as he or she may be of the
offences enumerated above, repents or surrenders himself
or herself to justice, shall be immune from punishment.
(6) Anyone who advocates or infuses Communism by
means of money shall be sentenced to penal servitude
ranging from three to five years. -Eastern News Agency".
A resume of outstanding incidents in the investigations
made and the action taken is given hereunder:
An organization with extremist tendencies which was
formed in 1916 established a secret bureau in Chengtu Road,
and rented a box in the American Post Office. Soon after
its inauguration, a real trade union was formed by local
painters who broke away from the guild organization which

3
they and their forbears had supported for centuries. A strike
amongst these workers took place soon afterwards, and it was
remarked that the organizers had coined Chinese equivalents for
such terms as "employee", "Capitalist", etc. The Electric
Workers' Union was then formed, and again it was remarked that
the leaders of the movement were well acquainted with the system
of organization adopted by European and American workmen. The
bureau in Chengtu Road closed after a few months, and activities
of the nature on which it was engaged were not again resumed
until 1919. In May of that year investigations made at the Ta
Tung Book Store, No. 119B Foochow Road, and the Oriental Book
Company, No. 84 Canton Road, resulted in the seizure of several
volumes of different books advocating the overthrow of the
present governmental system in favour of one based on Communism
or extreme socialism. Some of the books were comparatively
mild, but others were of pronounced anarchical tendencies and
favoured the subversion of all Government and law. The proprietors
of the stores were heavily fined, and a Cantonese, who acted
as the local wholesale agent for the books, was sent to prison
for six months.
Advertisements in the books showed that agents had been
appointed for their sale at schools as far apart as Peking
University and Lo Ying College near Swatow. There was no
conclusive evidence that any of the prominent political parties
were behind the propaganda, but in a signed statement made by
the Shanghai wholesale agent, he declared that his principal
was employed by a prominent official of the Kuomintang Party.
One of the most inflammatory of the books seized was
called "The People's Bell", and the fact that the Students'
Union of Peking and Tientsin gave that name to a paper which
they started on June 8 of that year was considered significant.
Later in the same year literature described as Bolshevist
emanating from this port was seized in the cities of Tientsin

4
and Peking and at places in the provinces of Hupeh, Anhwei and
Kwangtung. From intercepted correspondence it was further
ascertained that communist literature had also been despatched
in the latter part of 1919 to Chinese in England, France and
America who, in acknowledging receipt of the books sent, asked
for more. A number of letters from Nanking and from towns
and cities in Kiangse, Honan and Szechuen, containing demands
for pamphlets and papers were also intercepted by the Authorities.
The Bolshevist propaganda was again evident in 1921. On
June 4 in that year a number of Chinese of the student class
carrying flags emblazoned with violently worded mottoes,
entered the Hongkew Park where the Olympic Games were in
progress and proceeded to distribute leaflets advocating their
views. When an on-looker attempted to stop one of the youths
the latter drew an automatic pistol and fired several shots,
but fortunately without harmful results. The Police succeeded
in arresting six of the demonstrators, including the gunman
who was sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment and expelled.
These were each sentenced to 6 months imprisonment to be
followed by expulsion. Another was expelled and the case
against the sixth man dismissed. Other efforts by the Police
in that year to stop the pernicious propaganda included the
successful prosecution of four publishers and disseminators of
Communistic literature and the seizure and confiscation of
large quantities of handbills and pamphlets. Precautionary
measures also prevented a group of agitators from holding
meetings and processions on Labour Day, May 1.
In 1922 the Police continued to maintain vigilant
surveillance over Chinese political agitators. A vendor
of inflammatory literature, who had been detected in this
offence for the fourth time, was fined $500.00 at the Mixed
Court on January 6. On June 8, a search made at houses in
Taku Road showed that they were being used as the headquarters

5
of a group controlling three societies, known as the Non-Christian
Students' League, the Marx Literature Research Society and the
Young Men's Socialist Society. The shops of all three
organizations were found on the premises which also contained
a library of 500 volumes in Chinese, Japanese, Russian, English,
French, and German of a nature in keeping with the aims of the
organizations. The police also discovered handbills attacking
capitalism and Christianity - "its handmaid" -, and evidence that
some members of the group had travelled in Russia a short time
previously, and that others were corresponding with Russians
known to be in close relations with the Soviet agent at that
time in Peking. An order for the confiscation of the inflammatory
literature was made by the Mixed Court on June 20, but
unfortunately the Police were unable to bring home responsibility
for its ownership to any particular individual. They were
successful, however, in obtaining evidence against the chief
of a group called the Labour Secretariat, which had offices in
Chengtu Road. He was charged at the Mixed Court on June 9 with
inciting postal employees to strike and publishing inflammatory
articles in the Labourers' Weekly, and was sentenced to 5 months'
imprisonment and expulsion. The judgment of the Court also
included an order to have the offices of the paper closed. This
leader was probably the most active labour agitator who had
ever disturbed Shanghai. In addition to the sentence of
imprisonment and expulsion, he had previously been fined at the
Mixed Court for intimidating an agent engaged in recruiting
workers to replace the seamen on strike in Hongkong. It was
also known that he had taken an active part in organizing memorial
meetings in honour of Marx and other socialists. These meetings
were marked by the distribution of inflammatory handbills,
including one advocating the seizure of power by the Chinese
proletariat. The discoveries made in Taku Road and other

6
evidence previously obtained by the Police showed that the
anti-Christian movement had been used as a cover for communist
propaganda.
After a period of comparative quietness in the Winter of
1923 and the Spring of 1924, a revival of the Bolshevist
activities was noticeable in Shanghai towards the end of the
latter year. Closer co-operation among Russian elements was
secured by the concentration of all their offices in the
Consular Building. Efforts were also made to popularize the
movement by injecting into the propaganda appeals to Chinese
anti-foreign sentiments concerning unequal treaties, the
abolition of concessions and the cancellation of extraterri-
toriality - a set of demands which had been adopted as planks
on the Kuomintang platform at the beginning of the year. The
main local centre for the propagation of these views appeared
to be the Shanghai University. The premises of this school
were accordingly searched on December 9, 1924 when no less
than 189 different kinds of books advocating Communism or
dealing with some phase of extreme socialism were seized. A
store for the sale of some of these books was discovered in
the University compound. An application was made at the Mixed
Court on February 13, 1925, that Zau Lih Tsz, who was acting
President of the University, be expelled, and that the books
be confiscated. The Court ordered Zau to file a bond in the
sum of $1,000.00 to refrain from Bolshevist propaganda and
ordered the confiscation of the books. The literature seized
at the Shanghai University brought the total number of
different kinds of books on communist and extreme socialist
subjects, confiscated by the police between May 1918 and
March 1925, up to 1202. Of these 771 were in Chinese, 171 in
English, 39 in Russian, 8 in German, 144 in Japanese, 18 in
French and 1 in Spanish. The Police in the same period

7
successfully prosecuted 272 persons concerned in the
diffusion of Bolshevist literature and offences arising
out of the promotion of strikes. The history of these
cases shows that agitators devote their attention to the
exploitation subsequent to the commencement of strikes of
dissatisfaction already existing and in no case was evidence
available that a strike had been actually started by them.
As a matter of fact the disputes were invariably due to some
grievance either real or imaginary. The official inquiries
into the recent Japanese cotton mill strike tend to show
that the same happened in that instance.
Zau Lih Tsz(邵力子), who in addition to his
post in the Shanghai University, held the position of editor
of the Min Kuo Pao, was brought up on remand at the Mixed
Court on April 18, 1925 charged with breaches of the
Publication Law and with being a danger to the peace and
good order of the Settlement. The Court, which consisted
of Mr. Tajima, Japanese Assessor, and Magistrate Loh,
fined the accused $330.00 and expressed the opinion that
the article on which the charge was based was anti-foreign,
but neither Bolshevist or Communist.

March 10th, 1925.

CONFIDENTIAL.

Sir,

Representing members of the Japanese Chamber of Commerce, Shanghai,
I have the honour to express my sincere thanks for the invaluable
services rendered by your Council and its Police Force to the Japanese
residents during the regrettable strike which occurred recently in
the Japanese owned cotton mills here.

As it is explained in my last letter addressed you on 21st February,
the strike has been directed by some leaders of the Bolshevism
party as beginning of an expression of the Bolshevism campaigns in
China, and if it is permitted without any prevention, it will be sure,
as a matter of fact, that the movement of such kind would be appeared
so often in the future to degenerate into more fierce struggles which
will lead to possibilities of a breach of peace and order of the
International Settlement and its out-lying districts. In this
juncture, I have the honour to implore that you will kindly take up
the matter into your consideration to devise a constructive policy
with a view to checking any further menace of the welfare in this
part of China which controls in some respects the Commercial destiny
of nations.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,

( T. Tanabe. ),
Chairman.
Japanese Chamber of Commerce of
Shanghai.

S. Fessenden, Esquire,
Chairman,

February 22nd. 1925.

REPORT ON Attached.

Made by and Forwarded by Sub- Inspector Adams.

Sir:
I beg to report that on the February 10,1925,at about 10.35 A.M. a telephone message was received at this Station from No.9 Mill asking for assistance. Accompanied by D.S.Andrews,Sergeant Herdry and two Chinese Detective Constables,I immediately proceeded to the above Mill.

On entering the main Gates,we observed a large number of workers leaving quite peacefully,and coming from the direction of the offices were a number of coolies,carrying sticks and iron bars,who on seeing us,dropped same and mingling with the mill workers got away. Our party then split up,Sergeant Hendry and myself proceeded in the direction of the offices where a number of rioters were still running wild,leaving D.S.Andrews and his detectives in the compound. As we entered the office so we found the rioters had left by the back entrance,and made good their escape amongst the mill workers. The man named Kyi Siau S Ts(季小田子 )was arrested by D.S.Andrews,this man being in possession of an iron bar and appeared to be one of the worst offenders.

Receiving information that the strikers were proceeding to other mills,a telephone message was sent to Pootoo Road Station to this effect. Every effort was made to effect the arrest of the actual offenders,but owing to the difficulty under which we were placed at the time,in as much that the damage had been done before we were informed,and further more,the strikers received knowledge of our arrival and so defeated our ends by mixing with the large number of mill workers who after being intimidated were leaving the premises.

(周 金 生)
The following is the statement of Tau King Sung, D. C. I.'s Chauffeur.
native of ____________________ taken by me O.D.I. Burnside
at C.I.D. Headqrs. on the 16/2/25 and interpreted by Zung Zoong Oen.

At about 10p.m. on 15/2/25, I took the D. C. I. to
Van Wong Doo ( 梵 皇 渡 ), Jessfield. Inspector Gibson
who was there ordered me to pull the Station Car from out of
the Soochow Creek into which it had fallen. I replied
that I could not do so without instructions from Mr. Armstrong
who was then in a nearby factory. Inspector Gibson then
went away. In a little while, a plain cloth foreign
constable ( I was afterwards told that his number is "33" )
hustled me and told me to tow the Station Car from the Creek.
I replied, "This is Mr. Armstrong's Car and as the Soochow
Creek is deep, to pull the fallen car up might damage my car,
consequently I cannot obey your instructions without the D.C.I.'s
order." This Constable in plain clothes got excited at
my words and twice slapped me heavily on the face then kicked
me on the thigh. I cannot show any marks of injury.
During the time, the car key which I carried on my right first
finger was lost. Then I went to the factory to find the
D.C.I. but as he was talking with a number of Japanese, I was
not in a position to report the matter. At about 12 M.N.
the D.C.I. left the factory and ordered me to carry a wounded
person to a Japanese Hospital on Boone Road. When I returned
to the Central Station with the D.C.I., I reported the
occurrence to him. The key I subsequently found lying on
the floor of the driver's seat of the car.

Telling him to warn Pootoo Road Station as a precaution-

RECENT COTTON MILL STRIKE
HERE ALLEGED TO BE WORK
OF THIRD INTERNATIONAL

STARTLING DISCLOSURES OF BOLSHEVIST
ACTIVITIES MADE IN LOCAL
NEWSPAPER

SOVIET AGENTS DIRECTED STRIKE

Cessation Of Subsidies To Operatives' Committee
Said To Have Led To Failure Of Move

Startling disclosures, describing with circumstantial completeness, Communist connections with the recent strike at the Japanese cotton mills in Shanghai, which resulted in 31,000 operatives being thrown out of work and 22 mills closed, were published in yesterday's issue of the Shanghai "Mainichi," a Japanese newspaper. The paper quotes its evidence of Bolshevist influence behind the strike and states that the strike was carefully planned by the Third International and conducted by agents sent here for the purpose.

Anti-Japanese feeling among the Chinese and the complaints of ill-treatment of the operatives by the foremen were, the "Mainichi" states, exploited to the fullest extent to give stimulus to the strike, and a call was sent round to other labour organizations, the Chinese Communist party and students at radical colleges in Shanghai to render assistance. Funds were supplied by Soviet agents, but the obstacle which led to the return to work was the disappointment of the Soviet agent at the lack of unanimity among the operatives. For this reason, there was trouble on the third day and Soviet financial support, it is stated, was withdrawn.

According to a translation of the article by the Nihon Dempo news agency, the "Mainichi" published a document, signed by a Soviet official, who handed it to the strike committee. The document reads as follows:

INSTRUCTIONS FROM SOVIET
GOVERNMENT

"Apart from the instructions previously given, we are herewith giving you the following additional directions.

"1.—The strike committees which you have organized among yourselves are requested to act always in accordance with the dictations of their own conscience and to supervise the expenditure of funds that have been supplied from the Soviet Treasury.

"2.—It must not be forgotten that the attainment of the object in view (the strike) can only be effected through the co-operation of the Chinese, and the success of this co-operation depends largely upon the success of the strikes to be started by Chinese labour leaders.

"Before deciding upon entering the second phase of action, it is necessary to ascertain the results of the strikes. Therefore, it is imperative that they be started by February at the latest.

"3.—Emergency outlays (of funds) which have been made in connection with the strikes should be reported every time as it is necessary to report to the financial department the manner in which the money has been spent."

Soviet Lends Hand

This document was handed to the strike committee formed among the leaders of the operatives, and, says the paper, certain Soviet officials and Kuomintang members were ordered to assist, and several meetings were held before the strike was called. On January 31, one of the leading officials of the Soviet-Chinese Communist Party came up from Canton to attend a special meeting of the executive committee which had been convened. The meeting was attended by Soviet officials, including the head of the Propaganda Bureau, and Chinese labour agitators. At the meeting the Soviet officials insisted on the adoption of the measure planned by the Third International and the Propaganda Bureau, which was to start a general strike immediately. Permanent Soviet officials opposed this hasty action, suggesting that caution should attend all movements, but as the Chinese supported the general strike suggestion, the advocates of caution were overruled.

Everything was thus set for call-
ing a strike. A certain Russian,
formerly in the employ of the
Chinese-Eastern Railway, famous
as a specialist in strike questions,
was sent down from the north to
direct the strike, the "Mainichi"
states, and he set up local offices
from which he began to work to-
wards the object in view. From
the very first anti-Japanese feeling
and the cruelty complaints which
featured so largely among the
strikers' reasons for their action,
were seized upon as valuable pro-
paganda points and preparations
were made for calling the strike.

The reason why British mills
were not affected was because the
instigators of the strike were
aware that very firm and cordial
relations existed between the em-
ployers and the employees so any
strike appeal would fall on deaf
ears or, through the co-operation
between the employees and the em-
ployers, would soon reach the
knowledge of the employers and
the whole conspiracy would be ex-
posed.

Signal For Strike Given

A few days before the strike
began, the newspaper declares, a
meeting was held at one of the
Russian's homes in Broadway,
where the signal for the strike
was given. It was arranged that
the Nagai Wata Kaisha mills
should be the first field of action
and the sum of $3,000 was voted
from the Soviet propaganda funds
for this purpose. Chinese present
at the meeting also decided to
vote, on behalf of their organiza-
tions, support from the Kuomin-
tang Radical group, the Chinese
Seamen's Union, and the Chinese
Communist Party. Further, to
hoodwink the public and throw a
guise of sincerity over the con-
spiracy, it was decided to conduct
a campaign for funds among other
grades of Chinese workers, in tea
shops and other places.

The signal for the strike was
given and it was definitely laid
down, states the "Mainichi," that
all demands to be forwarded to the
employers should first be examin-
ed by the strike committee. The
strike started at the Nagai Wata
Kaisha on February 10 and thence
it spread to other mills until only
two remained open, while the dis-
orderly conduct of the strikers at
the other mills necessitated big
police guards.

Dissension Creeps In

Dissension crept into the de-
liberations of the strike agitators
on the third day of the strike. The
strike committee applied to the
Communist Committee for more
money, but this was refused, pre-
sumably because the Soviet officials
were disappointed at the lack of
unanimity among the strikers, only
a few of the mills closing at first,
the other operatives not striking
until a week later. Deprived of
financial support, the strike com-
mittee was helpless and was com-
pelled to allow the strike to drift
towards a settlement, of which
very mixed opinions are held re-
garding whether it was a victory
for the strikers or the employers.

The newspaper states that many
Chinese students participated in
the strike and met every night at
the home of one of the Russians
to receive instructions as to the
work to be done on the following
day.

MUNICIPAL POLICE
REPORT

In his report for February the
Commissioner of Police states:—
An agreement, which appears to
be nothing more than a reiteration
of the conditions under which the
employees formerly served, was
signed on the afternoon of Febru-
ary 26. The enthusiasm display-
ed by the Chinese officials when
real necessity for their inter-
vention had passed is, to say the
least, peculiar. Not only did they
fail to show any disposition to
help in the early stages when the
trouble might have been nipped in
the bud, but they suffered to con-
tinue in their territory an inten-
sive campaign of propaganda and
intimidation which was undoubted-
ly responsible for the large di-
mensions which the strike reach-
ed. The so-called agreement is
now being used by the agitators
to further a belief among the work-
ers that the strike was a success.
Boastful hand bills about the
victory gained are being dis-
seminated far and wide among the
mill workers. The agitators also
occupy their base in Chinese ter-
ritory without interference from
the Chapei Police, and the latest
news is to the effect that they are
calling for all mill workers to
register with a view to organizing
a new union. Had no agreement
been made, the agitators would
most probably have been discredit-
ed and a movement of this sort
would have been impossible.
